analysis.file_name: _We Could Hit An AI Air Pocket__ Deutsche Prices Superintelligence At $900 Billion... Per Training Run.pdf
analysis.title: "We Could Hit An AI Air Pocket": Deutsche Prices Superintelligence At $900 Billion... Per Training Run
key_insights: Deutsche Bank Research Institute (Adrian Cox, Oct 12, 20-page report 'AI boom or doom') tests the 'San Francisco Consensus' on superintelligence against physical constraints. Conclusion: the science might work, but the cost is very large and increasingly debt-funded.
DB estimates training 2026's top models took 10^26 to 10^27 FLOPs. An 'AGI-like model' needing three orders of magnitude more implies a 10^30 FLOP run.

Running one 10^30 FLOP training run on all of today's US AI infrastructure would take nearly four years. The infrastructure would need about 6GW, roughly 50% more than the four recently activated Vogtle nuclear units, at a cost of $300bn to $500bn.
Completing the run in four months on Nvidia Vera Rubin chips would need 7.8m chips and 26GW of facility power. DB puts that at $900bn today, with a rental-equivalent cost of $90bn.
If hardware cost trends hold, a 2030-era cluster able to do such a run would need about $200bn of compute and power hardware, for a training run costing about $20bn.

Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft and Oracle are set to invest almost $800bn of capex in 2026 and over $1 trillion a year through 2030 and beyond. That adds $4 trillion to $6 trillion of AI compute by 2030, enough for a 10^30 FLOP run 'with some comfort'.

DB's base case is that the AI economy excluding China will likely exceed $200bn of revenue in 2026, up from below $1bn in 2022. ZeroHedge calculates this is roughly a quarter of hyperscaler capex this year.

DB expects AI financing to shift from free cash flow and equity to debt. Capex is approaching the point where it is no longer covered by operating cash flow and net debt exceeds EBITDA, which raises exposure to rising rates and creditor appetite.

Alphabet posted its first quarterly free cash outflow in nearly two decades in its latest quarter while raising full-year capex guidance to $205bn. It also reported a $514bn backlog of contracted, not-yet-recognised data centre revenue.
Gartner (Oct 14) calculates $8.5 trillion of revenue is needed through 2030 versus no more than $3.6 trillion expected. ZeroHedge says this hit the market hard this week.

DB argues power, not chips, is the binding constraint. Grid connection queues, turbine lead times and transmission build take years, and substation transformer lead times are as long as three years. US politics has shifted toward slowing the AI build-out.
ZeroHedge expects labs to move to behind-the-meter generation: gas turbines on site near term, modular nuclear longer term.
DB says the thesis rests on scaling continuing to work and on recursive self-improvement (RSI). Yann LeCun and Ilya Sutskever are cited as skeptics of the LLM path.

METR's measure of software tasks frontier models can complete has risen to about 16 hours, from four minutes for GPT-4 in March 2023. DB notes a long road from 50% accuracy to the 99-100% needed for enterprise use.
DB lists brakes on runaway self-improvement: research is clock-bound, the real world defies verifiability, and Amdahl's law caps speed-ups.
DB's verdict: it is uncertain whether demand will be enough to pay upfront for the investment in achieving RSI that would justify it.
earnings_insights: Alphabet latest quarter (per DB, as reported): first quarterly free cash outflow in nearly two decades. Full-year capex guidance raised to $205bn. Contracted, not-yet-recognised data centre revenue backlog of $514bn.
risk_factors: Revenue shortfall versus capex: DeepMind's Sekhon warns of an 'AI air pocket' where expenditures happen but revenues do not show up.
Debt financing exposes hyperscalers to rising rates and creditor appetite as capex outruns operating cash flow and net debt exceeds EBITDA.
Power constraints: grid queues, turbine lead times, transmission build and three-year substation transformer lead times.
Scaling may stop working and recursive self-improvement may be limited, which would leave the capital wasted.
Political pushback against the AI build-out in the US.
geopolitical: US politics has shifted toward slowing the pace of the AI build-out, per DB.
cross_bank_references: Goldman's math on how much revenue is needed to justify $1.7 trillion in hyperscaler capex (Sep 27), referenced by ZeroHedge.

tension_points.bull_case: Hyperscalers plan over $1 trillion a year of capex through 2030, AI revenue excluding China is growing from below $1bn in 2022 to over $200bn in 2026, and Alphabet has a $514bn contracted data centre backlog.
tension_points.bear_case: AI revenue of about $200bn is roughly a quarter of 2026 hyperscaler capex. Gartner estimates $8.5 trillion of revenue is needed through 2030 versus no more than $3.6 trillion expected. Financing is shifting to debt as capex exceeds operating cash flow.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Capex no longer covered by operating cash flow and net debt exceeding EBITDA, with rising rates and weaker creditor appetite, would break the debt-funded bull case.
